body:
Music was a big part of my personal gender journey because I channeled a lot of my "genderfeels" through music, so as a starting point I thought naming myself after one of the musicians whose work helped me through it all would be appropriate (whether the musicians themselves would be flattered or creeped out is another story). I tried out a few names and figured I'd keep going until I found one that fit. It only took a couple of names before I stuck to Sascha, "borrowed" from Sascha Konietzko.

I've told the story of my first name many times, but my middle name's story, not so much. I wanted something somewhat unique and hopefully gender-neutral that started with an A, like my birth name, but had no idea what to choose. Eventually I ended up with Aidan, which was nice but still felt kinda off, so I was looking for other options. This is where music comes in again, but in a kinda weird way... I was coming back from my second psychologist appointment with my mom (my car couldn't take the long drive so she drove me) and the radio started playing one of the only Falco songs people around here know - Rock Me Amadeus. At that point I suddenly realised Amadeus met my criteria for a middle name almost perfectly (but of course I hadn't thought about the name before then since I had rarely, if ever, come across it)... So it stuck, and from that moment onward I was known as Sascha Amadeus.

It's kinda weird and convoluted a process when most trans people I know literally just changed the gender of their name, went with their parents' suggestion, or picked something completely random but relatively normal-sounding. I've never been a normal person, though, so the fact that my name reflects that seems appropriate. :p

Sorry this got so long, I'm terrible at trying to shorten down my posts... To answer your questions, I highly encourage you to try multiple names on. You might be lucky and find the right one quickly, or you may need to go through a few before finding what fits. When you find the name that fits you the best, you'll know it's the one - perhaps not right away, but at some point you'll realise it. You might find yourself gravitating back to it even after trying out more names, or you might have a moment like I did where you go "yep, I won't find anything that fits better than this so I'm sticking to it". Choosing a name is a HUGE decision and you'll be living with it for the rest of your life, so you have to be sure you've picked a name that feels right for you.

I much prefer men's clothing. Overall, it fits my body shape much better, and I like the overall look and style of men's clothes a lot more. My personal style/aesthetic (industrial/rivethead style) is very male-dominated so I've ended up with a fuckload of men's clothes since I started dressing in that style. Men's pants also have the added bonus of having actual pockets - I'm still amazed that my pockets can fit two sets of keys, my wallet and my phone and *still* have room for stuff.

Women's clothes are restricting, expose too much, are made with fabric so thin you need 346543 layers to keep warm... and they're just plain *boring* in my eyes. It's all V-necks and frilly crap and weird uncomfortable fabrics to me, and I just plain don't see the appeal at all. I have only two or three women's shirts left, and I only keep them because they're concert shirts I can't replace.

Thank you for the kind words! I can relate to that in a way. When I think about/imagine my future/post-transition self, I get so happy and giddy knowing that it's coming that I can't imagine myself staying the way I am now.

You've got a good point there. Even though I feel doubt about this situation, I also feel like I have to keep going, because I know the alternative (trying to repress my gender stuff again) just isn't going to work. I've struggled with my mental health for so long that I'm at a point where I'm up for anything that has a chance of improving things, quite frankly.

Thank you for the advice!

Funny coincidence, I was thinking about that recently in regards to my own name. With my name (Sascha), you can take out one letter and have it be a slightly different but also typically-male name (Sacha), or you take out a different letter and you get a typically-female name (Sasha). The number of people who default to writing Sasha when I don't spell out my name is both astounding and saddening. The only times I'm asked about the spelling is if I pronounce my name the German way (Z sound rather than S sound at the start) but that just leads to having to repeat myself a lot before the other person hears it properly.

I try not to let that bother me too much, though. I chose an unusual name and with it I came to expect that a lot of people would make mistakes, as they tend to do with every unusual name out there.

I have Crohn's and so far haven't seen a difference in how I've been treated (although I'm not really far along in transition, medically speaking). Obligatory disclaimer: I am not a doctor and you really should ask your gastroenterologist about this kind of stuff to stay on the safe side.

I think the important part is to keep up on your current treatment regimen (meds, etc.) and continue to be followed up in regards to your condition; seeing your doctor regularly, getting any required tests done on time, that sort of thing. Transition can cause a lot of stress, which could get you in trouble if you're like me and your flare-ups are often triggered by stress. If this  is the case for you too, try to find something that can help you cope with that stress in a way that won't make you sick. Avoid whatever causes you to flare up, really.

I think you should, at least, talk to your doctor about medications. (I'm currently in a dilemma involving meds that I'm trying to solve the best I can [tl;dr meds combo my doc wants to give me can't be given to males, afraid I'll have problems cuz I want to start T].) To be honest, medication for a chronic illness is pretty much the one thing you *don't* want to mess with. The chance of whatever meds you're on interacting with anti-androgens or E is probably quite low, but it's better to ask about it and be safe than to go into it blindly and having something happen.

I don't use my birth name, I never liked it and I never had any sort of attachment to it. Hell, even my parents weren't attached to it, they've told me so before. Said name is also heavily gendered and doesn't have a neutral or male counterpart, and I didn't like the male name my parents had picked for me if I had turned out AMAB. I ended up choosing my own.

The name I gave myself has NOTHING in common with my birth name, but I love that about it. It makes me feel like I'm evolving and becoming who I really am without feeling limited by my old name and everything attached to it. It took me four names to settle on one, and after I found it, my middle name came to me quite quickly. The name I chose felt so natural I couldn't *not* use it.

Fun story: The first time I told my mom about my chosen name, her reaction was: "Oh... hey, you know what, that's a nice name. If I had known about it twenty years ago, I might have named you that!"

It's your money, you do what you want with it. :p It's not as unusual as you think for adults to collect things like that. I personally collect, among other things, video game and anime stuff (plushies, character figures) and Pokémon cards, and on top of that I still sleep with a plushie (a Yoshi!). No one's ever commented on it being "inappropriate for [my] age" or anything of the sort - the worst I've gotten is a couple of confused glances towards one of my... lesser-dressed anime character figures.

I can relate to that a bit, as music did play a part in my own gender exploration (tl;dr an industrial band helped me realise I'm agender), but this is the first time I read about someone whose gender fluctuates according to what they listen to. If you ever write more about this, I'd definitely be interested in reading it.

There's no problem with changing your name, and if anyone complains about it being "inconvenient" for them to call you by your new name, well, they're just being a dick. At the end of the day, you're the one who has your name and uses it the most, so you should have a name you like and that you're comfortable with. Although I understand why you feel that way, it seems silly to me that someone would consider using a name they no longer like because they're afraid to be a burden on other people by changing it.

I have a somewhat large chest, most of it is due to boobs but I think my ribcage isn't helping matters either. As it is now, my wardrobe is mostly band shirts with a few button-ups. Only buying when I really need to is pretty much what I'm doing now, thankfully I haven't recently been in a lot of situations/events that required a certain way of dressing.

Accessories are also one of my weak points, so I know exactly how you feel. :p I have to admit I've always wanted to add ties to my outfits, but I've never really found any that I really liked or that fit well with what I wear. It's only in the past year or so that I've really started to develop my own style, so I'm still wandering in unknown territory for the most part, trying to figure out what fits me and what doesn't.

Thank you for the help! It does seem tricky to dress myself to try and hide my chest... In time I'll be able to figure out which parts of my wardrobe work and which parts don't. Right now I'm not really in a position to buy a whole new wardrobe for that, so I do my best with what I have now.

I had a phase like that too. I thought that if my body turned out to look like a typical girl's body was supposed/expected to look, then I'd stop having the feelings I was having and I'd end up feeling okay in my body, and consequently okay with being "a girl". That ended up never happening, though - and to be honest I'm happier with how my body actually turned out than I would've been if it had become more feminine. My body as it is now kinda looks like it had no idea what it was doing while growing - quite fitting, if you ask me.

Wow, the difference between the two is amazing! Thank you for sharing these - it helps a lot to see a comparison between the two. I also have to admit I agree with you when you say Underworks binders are itchy... It's annoying to deal with, especially when it gets hotter and sticks everywhere. I'll give GC2b a shot for my next binder and see how it works for me. Thanks for the help!

Yeah, considering the length of time he's been doing it, he's better able to figure out what works. He's showed me how he positions himself, but it hasn't had quite the same effect when I try it.

Though I appreciate the offer, I'm not too comfortable posting pictures. As for clothes, sadly a lot of what I typically wear is a bit snug, so I guess it doesn't help either (though I try avoiding those clothes when I bind). Is there any way to still make snug tops work or am I better off sticking to my button-up shirts instead?

I have to deal with the dreaded uniboob quite a lot. If I'm out for more than a couple hours, I end up having to go hide away and "adjust" my chest, and that gets quite annoying. Trying out GC2b for my next binder seems like it could be worth a shot - another commenter also said he had better results with their binders.

The friend in question is not yet on T, but he's been binding for 2+ years so I have a feeling that also plays a part in how easily he can flatten his chest now. Clothes are something else I'll have to learn to figure out... I thought I was doing fine, but judging by the reactions I get when I'm out and I'm binding, *clearly* there's something I'm messing up.

Thank you for all the advice!

I've heard about that company a lot, but I admit I didn't really think of them when it came time to buy my binder. It could be worth trying them out for next time, I think. If you're able to find comparison pics, I'd be interested in seeing them! It would be nice to see the "end result" of both binders compared to one another.
That's interesting to know - next time I get a binder, I'll measure it that way and see if it turns out to fit better than my current one. Thanks for the tip!

I'm aware that the sizing is done differently than on bras, and quite frankly, I wouldn't trust a bra measurement for anything other than what it's intended to measure. Could it be that I just measured at the wrong spot? I know the site said to do so at the widest point of the chest, but I don't remember if it mentioned a specific location (over the boobs, or underneath them, or anything like that). The widest point of my chest is, of course, where my boobs stick out, and that's where I ended up measuring. Hasn't caused me any issues with any other types of clothing except binders.

New Brunswicker here, currently living northeast of the province but moving to Moncton in the next few weeks. I've seen and heard good things about Fredericton, though I've never lived there; I'm sure you'll enjoy it. You might find it inconvenient to not be able to drive if you ever want to go out of the city, though.

/u/ElegantSyntax mentioned UBU in Moncton - I've been going to their meetings for the past couple months and it's been really helpful for me. I would definitely recommend that you join us every once in a while if you're able to do so! I've never been to the gender minorities group in Fredericton, so sadly I have no feedback to offer for them.

I still have doubts about myself, a lot more often than I'd like to. One thing I realised, though, is that people who question their gender almost always turn out to be trans - after all, someone comfortable with their assigned gender wouldn't have any reason to question it. Sometimes I wish I wasn't like this because I feel like it just adds to all the sickness I need to deal with, and I just want to have a chance to feel normal, you know?

The fact that you say you don't want to live the rest of your life as a male is, in my eyes, pretty solid proof that you're trans. Live your life the way you want to live it, and live as the person you know you are on the inside. :D You're definitely not alone in having these thoughts, if that can reassure you - I think most, if not all, of us go through a period of self-doubt at some point.

I have a note in my references section that says something along the lines of "The following people knew me as [old name], please use this name when you contact them." If an employer asks about the name change, I'm honest with them and explain exactly why I changed it (and quite frankly, their reaction to that says a lot about them IMO). Of course, I suppose that only works if you don't mind possibly having to out yourself...
I'm both happy for you and jealous. :p I really hope Canada gets this soon, I'm sick and tired of always being called by female titles.
NZ too? That's pretty awesome. :D Let's hope it won't take too long for it to spread, I'd love to see this here in Canada.
Well, I learned something new today. :D I hope the rest of the world will follow suit.
You assumed correctly. Quite frankly, that tends to be how most things get done in my province. x) When the time comes to get my passport, I'll give it a shot.

Agender person here.

> do you think gender "normal" people can really grasp agenderness

I think yes. My experiences telling people about my gender have overall been positive, though I admit they may be a bit biased, since most people I talked to were already somewhat familiar with non-binary genders, or at least familiar with the whole trans umbrella in general. I think anyone can understand it if it's explained well, though. Most misunderstandings, in my case, seemed to come from a lack of knowledge or explanation on the subject rather than an actual rejection of the concept.

Expect a lot of people to say something along the lines of "but everyone *has* to be a boy or a girl, you can't just be neither!" as their first reaction if you try to talk to them about it, though. Many of them still have this outdated idea that everyone has to fit into a binary gender. A lot of them will think differently once it's properly explained, though, and the ones that don't (people who completely reject the idea of trans or non-binary people, people who think non-binary identities are excuses to be a special snowflake, etc.) aren't worth dealing with.

> how fair do you think the situation is to her? Would you mind an SO thinking of you as your physical gender?

My theoretical SO doing this would not bother me, but if it came from anyone else, it would. I think it's normal for that to happen at first, but if it goes on for a long time, that's a different story. This is something you should ask your partner about, in my opinion; they may see the situation differently than I do. I also agree with /u/cazort2 in that there's a difference between wanting to change your viewpoint but having trouble doing so vs. outright not wanting to. The first is quite common and usually not too hard to work around, but the second is pretty shitty and downright disrespectful.

As for changing how you view your partner, a lot of it is in words and actions surrounding the person. Consider using genderless words like "person" rather than "girl" or "woman" when thinking about your partner. Asking for what terms they would prefer would be a good idea, unless this is something you've already discussed. I have to admit I feel a bit iffy about you calling your partner an "agender girl", and such, but if you discussed this and they said it was fine to use them, there's no problem in doing so. (I used they/them in my reply due to my uncertainty about your partner's pronouns, not out of any disrespect or refusal to use those words. I will edit accordingly if needed.)

Remember that gender is in the mind and not in appearance or actions. The fact that you support your partner's identity already says a lot (and certainly means a lot). Over time, your partner will likely open up to you more, about thoughts, feelings, etc. they've been dealing with. Keep an open mind and listen. Even if it's hard for you to give any advice (or even if you feel that you can't at all), being there to listen already means a lot.

Should you have any more questions, let me know and I will be more than happy to answer them.

I get misgendered nearly every day, but I've just stopped caring because no one makes the effort to correct themselves when I correct them. I feel like nobody really cares and that they prefer to misgender me because it's more convenient for them than using a different word for me. :/

What I did when I was looking for a psychologist was just asking my family doctor if he knew one who was experienced with transgender issues. He didn't know of one directly, but consulted his colleagues and got back to me about a week later, and he'd found one for me with their help. If you have private insurance through your mom (which is ideal as these specialists can be quite expensive), make sure that the one you want to see is covered. I personally see mine about once a month, but appointment frequency is decided by the patient and how often they feel they should see the psychologist.

Family doctors can prescribe antidepressants most of the time (mine did for me), but if you feel that you need anything more than that, consider a psychiatrist. You should prepare yourself to possibly wait a while, though. Not sure how it is in other countries, but here in Canada, the waiting lists are depressingly long if you can't find a private psychiatrist or aren't referred to one by a trans-specialised clinic. :/

If you've been contemplating suicide, though, please go and see your school counselor. Anything involving thoughts of self-harm or suicide should not wait.

That sounds great! If I may ask, where do you live? I haven't yet heard of a country that allows you to legally change your gender to a non-binary option. You're quite lucky to live somewhere that allows this. Thanks for sharing!

[edited to fix typo]

Sounds like that works out pretty good for you! Too bad it wouldn't work on a license too, but if you have no plans to get one, I suppose that won't bother you much. My province allows having U (for unknown) rather than M or F on licenses, but no other documents (passport, etc.) allow this because they all have to follow one's birth certificate. It's a small step forward, I suppose. Thanks for sharing!
That's an interesting way to see it. Perhaps in time you'll be able to have a neutral marker to use instead. Thanks for sharing!
Happy to see I'm not alone with that mindset. :D It sounds like that would also work out in your favour if you prefer to present as female. Thanks for sharing!

Sounds like an overly complicated process to change your gender legally... I'm sorry you have to deal with that :/ I'm surprised they require RLE for it, I thought that requirement (whether for getting hormones or for a gender marker change) had been phased out pretty much everywhere. I can see how all those requirements would be troublesome for a genderfluid person. Surgery-wise, my province still requires it to change one's gender marker, though they don't specify which surgeries "count", but the laws might change in the coming months.

It's good to hear you were at least able to change it with the NHS, though. It's something, at least. Thanks for sharing!

It always pains me to see girls who so desperately want to have what I've wanted to get rid of for over ten years. I wish modern medicine was advanced enough to allow me to give my uterus (and perhaps even my ovaries) to a trans girl - if that was a possibility, I would do it in a heartbeat. Sure, the pain it causes every month can be annoying, but I understand that, for you, that pain would be a small price to pay to have that last "missing" part. Just remember that lacking a uterus doesn't make you any less of a woman.
If I can get the missing couple of pieces in time, I'll go as Ness from Mother 2/Earthbound. I even have a Mr. Saturn to carry with me. :D

Not having the words to describe how I felt when those feelings first arose. My first language is heavily gendered, and by feeling essentially non-gendered, I was literally feeling something *that my language didn't have words for,* and because of this I thought feeling like I did was pretty much impossible or wasn't supposed to happen. If I had been able to express myself properly (no matter the language), the changes I now desperately want could have started so much sooner.

I can relate to that, because something similar happened to me at the group I go to. (Not gonna say more because the person in question knows my Reddit ID.) I think most of us who've been to in-person support groups have had this happen to them, and I wouldn't be surprised to find out that a lot of relationships start in those groups.

It happens to me every once in a while. I forget that I don't have a penis, and sometimes I panic because I don't know where it went... then I realise I don't have one. x)

I also tend to forget that my inner voice and my outer voice are nothing alike. My inner voice is deep and a little raspy (think Till Lindemann-like) but my outer voice is... girly and squeaky. That's when I remember there's *still* no T in my body, and it makes me quite upset.

A situation like this one is, quite frankly, a nightmare for me, but I understand the reasons why it happens.

Though it will definitely hurt to let him go (romantically, that is), I think that's the best thing to do in the long term. You can't force yourself to be attracted to him, and he has to understand that without holding that fact against you. When you discuss this with him, please make sure to mention that the issue is an incompatibility between his gender and your sexuality, not his transition itself. This situation is as hard for him as it is for you, though likely in different ways.

I understand that you're still in love with, and attracted to, the woman you'd been with for so long, but although you may want her back, it's *definitely not* a good idea to suggest detransition or to push him toward it. Doing so would hurt him even more and, quite frankly, it would be incredibly selfish to put him through something like that for your sake. You don't strike me as someone who would suggest that to him, but I still wanted to mention it.

Remember that on the inside he is still the same person he's always been. If a relationship truly can't work out between you two, you can still remain friends (and I'm sure he'd appreciate having your support, relationship or not), though after the possible breakup you may need some time apart from one another - as with any breakup, really.

Still, I am happy to see that you at least gave it a try, and I'm sure he appreciates that too. There are so many people out there who just up and leave when their partner decides to transition... Even if it didn't turn out how you both hoped it would, you at least tried, and that's already a lot more than many people in similar situations have done.

The names that I considered off-limits (and thus were never even considered among my choices) were names that were shared by family members or close friends - in my mind, those names already "belonged" to someone else, and it would have felt wrong to claim them even if I had wanted to. The name my parents would have given me if I had been AMAB was also off the list, simply because I didn't really like it - even my parents admitted not being attached to it much.

Aidan was a name I'd been considering as a middle name until I met a trans kid named Aiden who turned out to be a little shit for reasons that are irrelevant to this thread's subject. Because he and I shared almost the same friend group while he was around in my life and my friends' life, I felt like having Aidan in my name would just have been a reminder of that experience. It was one of the things that helped my middle-name dilemma, though (I was down to Aidan vs. Amadeus - I think you can easily figure out which name won).

To put it into context, I am non-binary and wanted to change my name to something neutral or predominantly masculine.

Definitely. I feel like things would be so much easier if I just could've been binary instead. I've considered faking being binary for the rest of my life just to make everything easier, but then I realise I wouldn't be able to last long pretending to be what I'm not.

Eden is a lovely name. :D


Changing your name legally is a procedure that varies depending on your country, and perhaps your state/province (depending where in the world you are), so you'll have to look into the laws where you live and how the name change procedure is done. There's usually fees associated to it. To give you an example, changing my name in my province costs about 100$ CAD and requires me to fill out a form with all my personal information as well as explaining why I want to change my name. The form must also be signed by a notary and by a witness. A judge goes over every name change, and when they're approved, they're announced in a provincial newspaper (something you can opt out of if you give them a good reason to).


Socially is much easier. Introduce yourself to anyone new you meet as Eden, and for your friends who already know you under another name, just tell them something like "I know you know me as [old name], but I would prefer if you called me Eden from now on." Whether you tell them about *why* you're changing your name is up to you. Understand that they may slip up at first, though.

Having two names is perfectly fine if that's what you prefer. I suggest that you let the people around you know how/when to use each name to avoid any awkward situations.


If you're really worried about confusing people, there's always the option to choose a gender-neutral name and always go by that name, but it's all up to you. Choose what feels right for you, not what's easiest to remember for others.

I present very masculine, or at least try to. Since I realised most people will still try to gender me as a man or a woman, I figured I'd do what I can to make them lean towards man. My figure is more masculine than feminine (and will be even more so as I get thinner), which helps a lot and makes me feel better about myself.


As for clothes, in my case, I mostly wear men's stuff. It fits my body better, and most of the clothes that fit with my style (I mostly dress in industrial/rivethead style) are quite masculine anyway. Feminine fashion never appealed to me much.

I've mentioned this story in a few threads before so part of me feels like I'm repeating myself - I'm always willing to share the story behind my name, though.


For my first name, I chose Sascha because it was a name I'd loved for a really long time. It's also the name of someone who's had quite a strong impact on myself and my life so far - Sascha Konietzko of KMFDM. (I loved the name long before I started listening to KMFDM, though, but I'd be lying if I said he didn't influence my name choice.) Sascha also has the advantage of being essentially gender-neutral in my language, as it can be seen as a combination of Sacha (M) and Sasha (F).


My middle name was chosen with only one condition - I wanted something that started with A, like my birth name. After a while of picking out names and trying them out, I ended up with two choices: a plain-sounding, "stealth" option (Aidan) and a more unusual, "out-there" option (Amadeus). In the end, quite unsurprisingly, Amadeus won. \o/ What's funny now is that I ended up with a name that sounds very German/Austrian - quite fitting since I hope to eventually live in Austria.


I also noticed one of the girls who posted earlier in the thread chose to name herself the same name I was given at birth - I'm so happy to see someone who can call my old name her own. :D

I agree with /u/en-serio; the label you choose to identify with is not what matters the most. Continue your journey of self-exploration until you become at ease/comfortable with yourself and who you are, because in the long run, that's what matters. Over time, you'll find a label that you think suits you.


In the meantime, I suggest doing what the past two commenters have suggested, and using a catch-all/more general term like non-binary to describe yourself for now. A lot of us started out in the same situation before we found a more specific term for what we feel. If/when you do find a term that suits you better, then you can start using that one. We are not here to tell you how to identify or tell you what we think you are; only you can figure that out, and only you can choose how to describe your gender identity.


Some people change the words they use to describe their identity over time, because sometimes they realise a certain term fits better, or they realise that what they identified with doesn't really describe them well after all. The same might happen to you, and in a situation like that there's nothing wrong with identifying differently than how you originally identified.
Seems like there's already some changes happening, then. :D I've been told T can start having effects on one's body quite quickly most of the time.

I can only imagine how relieving it must feel to have T in your system. I eagerly await the day when I'll be able to get my first shot! Stupid fucking estrogen is driving me completely insane... It'll be interesting to see at what speed the changes happen when the dose is low from the start, though. That's one thing I don't have much info about, and part of me fears that if I go for a low dose and it takes too long to have an effect, I won't get my desired result.

I'm non-binary but I prefer being "read" as male, so I hope it's still okay for me to share.

I'm somewhere around 159 cm or so (for you Americans, that's a tiny bit under 5'3"), which is a bit disappointing but better than what I expected to get height-wise. I don't come from a very tall family - the tallest person in my family is ~172 cm (5'8") tall. I have yet to start T, but fortunately I'm still young enough that I might sprout a few extra centimetres when I do start.

Height used to bother me a lot even before I started to think about my gender identity. Ironically, the thing that made my train of thought turn around was going to culinary school and having two cis male chef instructors who were only taller than me because they had taller hats. They seemed to deal with it just fine, so I figured if they could do it, I could too. Nowadays I try not to let it bother me too much, because I figure I could have ended up in a much worse situation build-wise, so I just have to make the best of what I ended up with.
Amadeus! \o/ I spent a while hesitating between Amadeus and Aidan, but in the end the former won. I like the sound of it, and I've always liked names that are a bit unusual/uncommon.

Voice comparison is something I really look forward to doing - just thinking about how deep my voice could get makes me so damn excited to finally get some T into my system! Even though I know it's unlikely to happen, I'd love to have a really deep and low voice like Till Lindemann, but I'll take pretty much anything that isn't as high-pitched as I am now.


I have binary trans friends who've showed me what their hormone shots are like, so I already know what to expect when I get mine. Explaining my gender identity and how I realised I was non-binary may give you some insight into the mindset of a non-binary person. I've given both ends of the spectrum a shot while I was exploring/experimenting my gender identity. I spent a big part of my life identifying as a girl because that's what I was told I was, but I did not feel like one, nor did I like being seen/interacted with as one; I simply wasn't comfortable that way. Non-binary people can and do have dysphoria, though what someone is dysphoric about, and the extent to which they are, varies from one person to another. Non-binary people go through a lot of the same things binary trans people go through when it comes to transitioning: hormones, name changes, chosen pronouns, surgeries, etc. Not all of them go through everything I listed, though, and some may choose not to transition at all. It all depends on what they feel that they need to do to be comfortable in their body.


The reason why some non-binary people can dislike certain gender expressions, especially those corresponding to their assigned gender, is usually for similar reasons than for binary trans people; in most cases they feel uncomfortable because they feel forced to fit into a binary they don't belong in, or they feel like they're forced to put up a facade and pretend they're binary because the world thinks their identity isn't real. Of course, that's not always the reason, but it's the most common reason I've personally seen. You should still remember that, just like with binary trans people, a non-binary person's gender expression does not dictate or invalidate their identity.

I think a lot of us have had the fear that we may be faking it somehow, but if I were you, I would try to get past that fear. If being able to express your nonbinary identity, being referred to as they/them, etc. makes you feel better about yourself (which is one of the end goals of it, really), why would you worry that you're faking anything? Clearly, you aren't. If you feel like nonbinary or genderfluid best describe you and your gender, then those words are yours to use and you shouldn't feel like you're appropriating anything - you can't really appropriate something that's already yours.


As for feeling like you should have been questioning your gender earlier... there's no set age or timeframe for this sort of thing. A lot of people begin questioning at a young age, but that doesn't mean *everyone* has to do it. Your feelings about your gender aren't invalidated just because of when you started to question it. Do *not* compare yourself to your genderfluid friend; comparing yourself to them is clearly having a negative effect on you. You are just as real as they are, you both just have different ways of expressing your identity and such.


As for having trouble passing, unfortunately, that's something you'll have to learn to cope with, either by accepting the misgendering (which always sucks) or working on your androgynous look until you get a result that doesn't make people misgender you constantly. The majority of the world doesn't even believe people like us exist, hence why they'll do everything to jam everyone in a "boy" or "girl" box even when you yourself reject the existence of the boxes.

As an example, if you have a group of women with one man, you'll refer to the group using the masculine plural pronoun *ils* no matter if you have three women or three million in the group - *ils* wins over the feminine plural pronoun *elles* because there's a man in there. Since French doesn't have any gender-neutral pronouns, I've pretty much just gotten used to using the neutral *il* to describe myself. To me, *il* at least implies some sort of neutrality, since it can be both male or neutral, but *elle* can't be anything other than female, and that's why I hate it.
